prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "QUALCOMM INC/DE" (ticker QCOM), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "QCOM", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: QUALCOMM Incorporated
result.industry: Wireless and edge-computing semiconductors and patent licensing
markets: IoT, industrial, XR and wearables chips
Data center AI accelerators, custom silicon and connectivity (AI200/AI250, Alphawave)

mission.statement: Qualcomm engineers human progress. We relentlessly innovate to enable intelligent computing everywhere.
mission.source: CEO message, Qualcomm 2023 Corporate Responsibility Report
mission.plain: Qualcomm wants to invent the chips and wireless technology that let smart, connected devices work everywhere.

about.plain: Qualcomm designs the 'brain' chips and wireless chips that go inside many phones, cars and gadgets. Its Snapdragon chips help Android phones run apps, take photos and connect to 4G and 5G networks. It also owns thousands of patents on how phones talk to cell towers, and phone makers pay it a fee for using them. It does not make the chips itself: factories like TSMC and Samsung build them from Qualcomm's designs.
about.customers: Phone makers like Samsung, Xiaomi, Honor and Apple, car makers like BMW and GM, PC makers, and big cloud companies.
about.everyday: If you own a premium Android phone such as a Samsung Galaxy, it very likely runs on a Qualcomm Snapdragon chip, and nearly every 4G/5G phone pays Qualcomm a patent fee.

money.plain: Snapdragon processors and 5G modems for smartphones
chips for PCs, headsets, smart glasses, wearables, Wi-Fi and factories
royalties phone makers pay to use its wireless patents
chips for car dashboards, connectivity and driver assistance
Snapdragon X processors for thin, long-battery laptops
AI200/AI250 inference accelerators, custom chips for cloud giants and high-speed connectivity

result.summary: Qualcomm has a real but narrowing moat: its portfolio of essential 4G/5G patents earns a toll on almost every phone sold (Apple and Huawei both renewed or signed licenses in 2025-2026), and its Snapdragon chips lead premium Android phones thanks to decades of modem and low-power design know-how. But handset chips are cyclical and concentrated, Apple is replacing Qualcomm modems with its own, MediaTek ships more phone chips, and FY2025 revenue ($44.3B) was barely above FY2022 ($44.2B), so the advantage protects profits more than it drives growth.

pricingPower.evidence: Licensing royalties have held for decades despite antitrust challenges, and in July 2026 management said it is raising prices by double digits across end markets to offset memory and input-cost inflation; however, gross margin slipped from 60.7% in FY2020 to 55.4% in FY2025 and Android handset chip revenue was expected to fall about 20% in 2026, showing limits when volumes weaken.

moats.evidence: Its standard-essential cellular patent portfolio produced $5.58B of QTL licensing revenue in FY2025, with license renewals from Apple (announced Sept 24, 2026, effective April 2027) and a new broad cross-license with Huawei (Oct 5, 2026); the Snapdragon brand is a marketed selling point for premium Android phones.

Phone and car makers build software, RF designs and carrier certifications around Snapdragon platforms over multi-year cycles, but large customers do switch: Apple moved to its in-house C1 modems and Samsung uses Exynos and MediaTek in some models.
Licensing and Android developer tools create some ecosystem pull, but more Snapdragon users do not directly make the product more valuable to other users.

About $9.0B of annual R&D (FY2025) spread over hundreds of millions of chips lets it fund leading-edge 3nm designs and modem development that few rivals can match, though MediaTek competes on cost with a similar fabless model.
The smartphone processor market supports several vendors (MediaTek 31%, Qualcomm 23%, Apple 19%, UNISOC 13% of Q2 2026 shipments per Counterpoint), so it is not a natural monopoly.
Its integrated licensing-plus-chips model is distinctive, but incumbents like NVIDIA, Broadcom and MediaTek face no structural barrier to responding to its moves into PCs, cars and data centers.

Over three decades of cellular modem expertise (CDMA through 5G Advanced) is very hard to replicate: Intel exited 5G modems in 2019 after years of losses, and Apple spent years and a $1B Intel modem acquisition before shipping its own C1 modem in 2025.

Its patent portfolio, largely built on contributions to 3G/4G/5G standards, is an exclusive asset that rivals must license, although older patents expire and newer 5G/6G contributions are shared with Huawei, Ericsson and Nokia.

customers.evidence: Major OEMs keep coming back (Samsung's Galaxy S flagships ship with 'Snapdragon for Galaxy' chips and Apple renewed its patent license), but relationships are transactional and concentrated: Apple is phasing out Qualcomm modems, with Qualcomm's share of the upcoming iPhone modems now expected well below 20%.

talent.evidence: Qualcomm is a respected engineering employer in San Diego and globally with a deep wireless R&D bench, but it is not on recent top employer rankings and has carried out periodic layoffs, while AI chip rivals such as NVIDIA compete aggressively for talent.

product.evidence: Snapdragon 8 Elite-class chips are widely regarded as the fastest and most efficient Android processors and its X-series 5G modems are industry-leading; it is also winning in cars (FY2026 automotive exit run-rate target raised to about $7B) and launched AI200/AI250 data center accelerators in Oct 2025.

competitors.name: MediaTek
competitors.note: Largest smartphone SoC vendor by units; competes in Android phones, Wi-Fi/IoT, Chromebooks/PCs, auto cockpits and custom data center ASICs.

competitors.name: Apple
competitors.note: Former modem customer now replacing Qualcomm with its in-house C1 modems; its A-series chips compete for premium phone share.

competitors.name: Samsung Electronics (System LSI / Exynos)
competitors.note: Exynos processors and modems compete for slots in Galaxy phones; also a key customer and foundry partner.

competitors.name: UNISOC
competitors.note: Chinese low-cost smartphone and IoT chipmaker serving entry-level phones.

competitors.name: Huawei (HiSilicon)
competitors.note: Kirin chips power Huawei phones in China, removing a former Qualcomm customer; also a 5G patent licensor.

competitors.name: Broadcom
competitors.note: Wi-Fi/Bluetooth connectivity, RF filters and custom AI ASICs for hyperscalers.

competitors.name: NVIDIA
competitors.note: Data center AI accelerators, Arm PC chips and automotive (DRIVE Thor) platforms.

competitors.name: Intel
competitors.note: x86 laptop processors versus Snapdragon X; automotive via Mobileye.

competitors.name: Advanced Micro Devices
competitors.note: PC processors and data center AI accelerators.

competitors.name: Arm Holdings
competitors.note: Supplier of the Arm architecture and now its own chips; litigation opponent in Delaware.

competitors.name: Marvell Technology
competitors.note: Custom data center silicon and high-speed connectivity, competing with Qualcomm's Alphawave unit.

competitors.name: NXP Semiconductors
competitors.note: Automotive processors and connectivity, industrial IoT.

competitors.name: Mobileye
competitors.note: Driver-assistance chips competing with Snapdragon Ride.

estimates.name: MediaTek (estimate: NT$595,966M converted at about NT$32/USD)

threats: Apple replacing Qualcomm modems with its in-house C1 modems; Qualcomm expects FY2027 Apple product revenue below its earlier forecast of slightly more than $2B.
Memory price spikes and supply constraints cutting smartphone demand: management expected the 2026 handset market down low teens and Android QCT revenue down about 20%.
Samsung's Exynos regaining Galaxy slots (Samsung reached 9% of smartphone SoC shipments in Q2 2026) and MediaTek's push into premium phones.
Huawei and other Chinese OEMs designing their own chips amid US-China tensions and export controls.
Arm litigation and licensing terms: a Delaware jury in Oct 2026 split the claims and awarded Qualcomm only $2, leaving royalty issues for the judge.
Execution risk in data centers against NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom and Marvell, with custom-chip margins expected to dilute QCT gross margin by 1.5-2 points.
Regulatory and antitrust scrutiny of its licensing model and acquisitions.

ceo.name: Cristiano Amon
ceo.background: Electrical engineer (UNICAMP, Brazil); joined Qualcomm in 1995 and ran its chip business and served as president before becoming CEO in June 2021

c1.evidence: Qualcomm leads premium Android processors and cellular patents, but smartphones are a mature market (FY2025 revenue $44.3B vs $44.2B in FY2022); it is a challenger, not the leader, in faster-growing AI data center and Arm PC chips.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Snapdragon for best-in-class modems, power efficiency and AI performance built on 30+ years of wireless R&D, which is hard to copy, but Apple, Samsung and Huawei have shown that large customers can build in-house alternatives.

c3.evidence: The Snapdragon brand is known to phone enthusiasts and advertised by Samsung and Xiaomi, but most ordinary people don't recognise Qualcomm the way they know Apple or NVIDIA.

c4.evidence: Its stated purpose 'Qualcomm engineers human progress' and the goal of 'intelligent computing everywhere' are tied to genuine contributions to 3G/4G/5G standards, but management messaging focuses heavily on diversification targets like $40B non-handset revenue by FY2029.

c6.evidence: “Snapdragon, 5G, patents, smartphone chips”: the impression is mostly positive about its technology, mixed with a reputation for aggressive licensing that drew antitrust fines and Apple litigation.

c7.evidence: Its markets are large and riding on-device AI, connected cars and AI data centers: management targets $40B of non-handset revenue by FY2029, including more than $15B from data centers, while automotive revenue grew 61% year over year in Q3 FY2026.

c8.evidence: It is extending its low-power Snapdragon and connectivity technology into PCs (Snapdragon X), cars (Digital Chassis), robotics, XR glasses and data centers via AI200/AI250 and the Alphawave and Modular acquisitions.

m1.evidence: Cristiano Amon has articulated a clear vision since 2021 of Qualcomm as an 'intelligent edge' and AI computing company beyond phones, setting long-range targets for auto, IoT, PCs and data centers.

m2.evidence: Amon is not a founder but a 30-year Qualcomm veteran (joined 1995) who has pushed long-term diversification bets, though the company still runs with large buybacks and dividends ($12.6B returned in FY2025).

m4.evidence: There is no clear public evidence either way that Amon leads in a distinctly servant-leadership style toward employees and customers.

m5.evidence: Qualcomm keeps an engineering culture that produced Snapdragon, 5G modems and automotive platforms, but it has relied on acquisitions (Nuvia 2021, Alphawave 2025, Modular 2026) for key CPU and data center capabilities.

m6.evidence: Amon is an electrical engineer who led Qualcomm's chip (QCT) business and personally launches Snapdragon products at events like Snapdragon Summit.

m7.evidence: No controversies stand out, but there is limited evidence of Amon pursuing goals beyond the business beyond Qualcomm's Wireless Reach philanthropy programmes.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Amon giving a commencement speech at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university.

m8b.evidence: Amon is an energetic, well-known keynote presence and a Brazilian-born tech leader, but he lacks the iconic public persona of Elon Musk or Jensen Huang.

m9.evidence: Under Amon revenue rose from $33.6B (FY2021) to $44.3B (FY2025) and automotive grew from $975M to $3.96B, but revenue fell 19% in FY2023 and FY2026 is expected to decline about 3%.

m10.evidence: Qualcomm is not known for frugality; it spends about $9B a year on R&D and pays for marketing such as Snapdragon sponsorships.

c10.evidence: Its cellular inventions and chips underpin how billions of people use mobile internet, since nearly every 4G/5G phone uses Qualcomm-licensed technology.

p2.evidence: Designing leading-edge 5G modems and 3nm phone processors is extremely hard, as shown by Intel exiting 5G modems in 2019 and Apple taking years to ship its own modem.

f1.evidence: Revenue was $23.53B (FY2020), $33.57B, $44.20B, then fell to $35.82B in FY2023 before $38.96B (FY2024) and $44.28B (FY2025): up in four of the last five years, with FY2026 tracking slightly lower.

f2.evidence: Gross margin fell from 60.7% (FY2020) to 55.4% (FY2025); operating margin rose from 26.6% to 27.9% but peaked at 35.9% in FY2022.

f3.evidence: At June 28, 2026 debt was $15.27B against $8.30B of cash and marketable securities, but that debt is only about 1.1x FY2025 operating cash flow of $14.01B, and equity is positive at $27.66B.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $6.26B (FY2020) to $12.36B (FY2025) and operating cash flow from $5.81B to $14.01B, though with a dip in FY2023 operating income.

v1.evidence: Snapdragon is the default choice for flagship Android phones because of its speed, efficiency and modem quality, but in the overall phone chip market Apple's in-house chips and MediaTek's cheaper chips are strong alternatives.

v2.evidence: Qualcomm is a respected engineering employer but does not appear in recent top employer rankings such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.

c5.evidence: If Qualcomm vanished, Android phone makers, carmakers and the 5G industry would lose a key chip supplier and a central inventor of cellular standards, delaying devices for hundreds of millions of people.
